reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A brain arteriovenous malformation is an abnormal tangle (nidus) of vessels where arteries connect directly to veins without an intervening capillary bed
The commonest serious presentation is intracranial haemorrhage, which may be intracerebral, intraventricular, or subarachnoid
Seizures are another frequent presentation, and some patients report chronic headache or progressive focal deficits
The high-flow shunt can cause a steal effect and venous hypertension, contributing to symptoms even without bleeding
Digital subtraction angiography is the reference standard for defining the feeding arteries, nidus, and draining veins, complementing CT and MRI
Grading systems that account for size, venous drainage pattern, and eloquence of adjacent brain help estimate surgical risk
Treatment options include microsurgical resection, endovascular embolisation, and stereotactic radiosurgery, used alone or in combination and individualised to the lesion
An associated flow-related aneurysm may coexist and can itself be a source of haemorrhage
reference.pathophysiology: A cerebral arteriovenous malformation is a congenital vascular anomaly in which feeding arteries drain directly into veins through a nidus of abnormal channels, bypassing the normal capillary network. The absence of intervening capillaries exposes the draining veins to high arterial pressures and flow, causing vessel wall changes and predisposing to rupture. Diversion of blood through the low-resistance shunt can reduce perfusion of surrounding brain (vascular steal), while venous hypertension and gliosis contribute to seizures and focal deficits. Haemorrhage results from rupture of the fragile nidus, draining veins, or associated aneurysms.
additionalInvestigations: CT and CT angiography to detect haemorrhage and vascular abnormality
MRI and MR angiography to localise the nidus and assess surrounding brain
Digital subtraction angiography to fully characterise angioarchitecture and any associated aneurysm
EEG when seizures are a prominent feature
redFlags: Acute intracranial haemorrhage with headache, focal deficit, or reduced consciousness
New or worsening seizures, especially with focal neurological signs
Evidence of an associated flow-related aneurysm raising rupture risk
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or rapid neurological deterioration
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on whether the malformation has bled, its size and location, and its venous drainage; haemorrhage carries significant morbidity and a risk of recurrent bleeding, whereas complete obliteration by surgery, radiosurgery, or embolisation can substantially reduce future haemorrhage risk.
pitfalls: Assuming all subarachnoid haemorrhage is aneurysmal and overlooking an underlying malformation
Underestimating the risk contributed by an associated aneurysm
Failing to fully characterise angioarchitecture before choosing treatment
Attributing new seizures or deficits to other causes without vascular imaging
management: Definitive obliteration by microsurgical resection, stereotactic radiosurgery or endovascular embolisation, selected according to Spetzler-Martin grade
Multimodal treatment in complex lesions, using embolisation as an adjunct to surgery or radiosurgery
Acute haemorrhage management with intracranial pressure control, reversal of any coagulopathy and neurosurgical evacuation of significant haematoma
Antiepileptic drug therapy for seizures associated with the malformation
Blood-pressure control and symptomatic management of headache
Surveillance angiography to confirm complete obliteration and detect recurrence
Neurovascular multidisciplinary decision-making on whether to treat or observe, weighing intervention risk against natural bleeding risk in unruptured lesions
